problem: The conclusion (waiting on turn==i is wrong) is right, but the stated reason is false. With turn==i written in the wait, if both flags are true only one process passes: Pi passes when turn==j, and turn cannot equal j for both i=0 and i=1 at once. Both processes never pass together in that state, so the given explanation misleads students about how the failure happens.
fix: The failure comes from one process reading the other's flag before it is set. P0 sets flag[0]=true, sets turn=1; P1 has not set flag[1], so P0 sees flag[1]=false and enters. Then P1 sets flag[1]=true, sets turn=0; P1 tests flag[0]=true and turn==1 (turn is 0, so false) and also enters. Both are inside, so mutual exclusion fails.

problem: The answer says that when both flags are true both conditions can be false. They cannot: with both flags true exactly one of the two conditions is false, exactly as in the correct version. The answer gives a wrong justification for a correct conclusion.
fix: The bug shows when the other flag is read before it is set. P0 sets flag[0]=true and turn=1, sees flag[1]=false, and enters; P1 then sets flag[1]=true and turn=0, sees flag[0]=true but turn==1 false (turn=0), and enters too. Both are in the critical section, so mutual exclusion fails.

problem: The last sentence, 'Waiting on turn==i would let both pass', is technically wrong. With turn==i and both flags true, exactly one process still passes; the mutual-exclusion failure of that variant needs one process to test before the other sets its flag.
fix: Keep the first part: turn==j gives the other process priority, so when both want entry i waits and only j enters. Replace the last sentence with: the loop must test turn==j, because with turn==i in the loop both processes can enter when one reads the other's flag as false before it is set.

problem: The claim that initializing turn to i 'breaks the tie' is not true. Both processes always write turn before testing, so the value at test time is the last value written; the initial value of turn cannot affect who enters.
fix: Drop the initialization clause. Say instead: testing turn against the wrong process breaks the tie, because process i must set turn=j and wait while turn==j.
